background.definition: The radius is the forearm bone that extends from proximal to the thumb of the wrist to the lateral elbow. The ulna is a long bone that is prismatic in form, found at the medial side of the forearm, parallel with the radius. The humerus is a long bone in the arm that runs from the shoulder to the elbow. A fracture is a structural break in the continuity of the bones, the epiphyseal plates, or cartilaginous surfaces of these structures.

list.listitem: The majority of fractures of the forearm are caused by accidental falls.
Trauma and falls are the cause of most proximal humeral fractures.

In community-dwelling elderly men and women, the independent risk factors for sustaining a forearm and/or a proximal humeral fracture are: femoral neck bone mineral density, falls, and dietary calcium intake.

The risk of fractures is decreased by the use of beta blockers, alone or in combination with thiazide diuretics, supporting the use of these agents in patients with hypertension, especially if they are at risk of developing osteoporosis.
Take note of history of direct blow to forearm, or a fall on an outstretched hand or directly on forearm. C
Consider the elbow extension test to rule out elbow fracture. B
Get anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique x-rays for most suspected fractures. C
Usual mechanism is fall on an outstretched hand or direct blow/trauma to radius, ulna or humerus.
In general, there will be points of localized pain, swelling, ecchymosis, deformities, tenderness on the forearm or arm, and pain with movement of joints where fractured bones are involved.
Note age of patient and remember implications of injury for children and older adults while evaluating.

Take note of history of direct blow to forearm, or a fall on an outstretched hand or directly on forearm. Note point of localized pain, swelling and tenderness on forearm; check for fractures of ulnar styloid, dorsal prominence of ulna. Also note if open or closed, and consider any break or puncture of the skin evidence of an open fracture until proven otherwise.
Neurologic examination: assess 2-point discrimination, having the patient sign "OK" to evaluate median nerve, wrist extension (radial nerve), and finger abduction (ulnar nerve).
Vascular examination: capillary refill time, radial pulse.
Test shoulder, wrist and elbow range of motion; check for pain with rotation. Significant humeral shaft displacement may result with upper arm shortening.

The elbow extension test (asking the patient to fully extend the elbow) has a high sensitivity for ruling out elbow fracture (96.8% (95% CI 95.0, 98.2) but is not very specific (48.5% (95% CI 45.6, 51.4); half the patients who tested positive were fracture free. A second study confirmed the high sensitivity.

Strong muscle contractions from high-velocity throwing or arm wrestling may also lead to humeral fractures. Moderate to severe shoulder pain may be a sign of humeral fracture. Patient will tend to hold affected arm adducted against side.
Get anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique x-rays for most suspected fractures.
Please see and for additional detail regarding imaging, and for the diagnostic approach.

Portable ultrasound use in the emergency department by "minimally trained clinicians" (e.g. 15 minutes of training identified 37 of 42 fractures) (90% sensitive, 96% specificity). In this same study, the level of agreement among multiple observers was 96%.
Another study directly comparing radiography with point of care ultrasound found excellent sensitivity and specificity of POCUS.
illustrates a suggested approach to management. In particular, it stresses the differences in terms of treatment as correlated with the location of the fracture.
Please see treatment algorithm in . C
If neurovascular compromise is evident, refer immediately to orthopedic surgery and consider closed reduction, always under adequate analgesia. C
Casts extending above the elbow or below the elbow have comparable outcomes in children with uncomplicated forearm fractures. B

A splint provides better functioning and similar pain relief compared with a plaster cast in children with distal radioulnar fractures, and refracture did not occur with either treatment. A Cochrane review supports use of removable splintage for buckle fractures. B
Use antibiotics in open fractures of the limbs and consider Vitamin C to prevent reflex sympathetic dystrophy in extremity fractures. B

It is unclear which conservative methods for treating distal radius and ulnar fractures in adults are superior; physicians should use techniques they are familiar with and are cost-effective, considering patient preferences and circumstances, as well as risk of complications. B

The evidence is unclear regarding which method of anesthesia is superior in the treatment of distal radius fractures in adults, although hematoma blocks appear to provide poorer analgesia and can compromise reduction. B
The incidence of infections in open fractures of the limbs is reduced by antibiotic use.

One study found that 500 mg of vitamin C for 50 days may help prevent reflex sympathetic dystrophy. However, this was not found in a second study with 336 patients randomized to vitamin C 500 mg or placebo for 50 days after distal radial fracture.
An RCT with 134 patients with distal radial fracture randomized within 2 weeks of surgery to vitamin C 500 mg or placebo found no impact on range of motion, function, or pain outcomes.

The best method of treatment for isolated fractures of the ulnar or humeral shaft in adults has not been established. A randomized controlled trial compared surgical with non-surgical treatment in 231 patients with displaced proximal humerus fracture. At 2 years, there was no difference in Oxford Shoulder Scores (39 vs 38 points) and no difference in physical function score or complications. There were 10 medical complications in the surgical group. At 5 year follow-up of 176 patients from the original cohort, there was still no significant difference in outcomes.

Another randomized trial identified 82 adults with closed, unilateral displaced humeral shaft fracture adn randomized them to surgery with open reduction/internal fixation or functional bracing. At 12 months there were no significant differences between groups with regards to outcomes. About 1 in 6 participants initially assigned to non-surgical treatment crossed over to surgery during the trial. Complications included non-union in 11 non-surgical patients, and temporary radial nerve palsy in 3 assigned to surgery.

A Cochrane review identified 31 studies with 1941 participants addressing the treatment of proximal humeral fractures. They conclude that there is moderate to high quality evidence that outcomes are not superior at 1 to 2 years for patients undergoing surgical repair of displaced proximal humeral fracture of the neck compared with non-surgical treatment.

A network meta-analysis of 10 RCTs and seven observational studies concluded that the likelihood of radial nerve injury was lowest for minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis, followed by open reduction and plate osteosynthesis, and was highest for intramedullary nailing. Similar results were found for the likelihood of non-union.
A randomized trial in 88 patients 60 years and older with a displaced 2 part humeral fracture found similar outcomes between surgical and conservative (sling or collar cuff for 3 weeks) management.
A secondary analysis of a randomized trial found that time from trauma to surgery did not affect outcomes.
A study randomized 124 patients with proximal humeral fracture to reverse total shoulder arthroplasty or open reduction/internal fixation. After 2 years outcomes favored arthroplasty.

There is some evidence supporting the use of external fixation and pinning for distal radius fractures in adults, but their precise roles and methods have not been established, and it is unclear whether long-term outcomes will be consistently better. A randomized trial comparing volar locking plate with conventional percutaneous fixation in 130 patients with displaced distal radial fracture found faster recovery with the latter, but no long-term difference in function at one year. An RCT comparing volar locking plate with external fixation (and optional K-wires) in patients age 50 to 74 years with dorsally displaced radial fracture found no difference in outcomes at one year.

A meta-analysis identified 6 RCTs with 561 patients randomized to either volar locked plating (VLP) or closed reduction and casting (CRC). At follow-up, the Disabilities of the Arm Shoulder and Hand scores were better in the surgery group (9 points at 3 months, 6 points at 1 to 2 years) but these differences did not meet the criteria of 10 points for a minimally clinically important difference.
The rate of subsequent removal of volar locking plates was 9% in a systematic review.

It is unclear which conservative methods for treating distal radius fractures in adults are superior, and so physicians are encouraged to use techniques they are familiar with and are cost-effective, considering patient preferences and circumstances, as well as risk of complications.

The evidence is unclear regarding which method of anesthesia is superior in the treatment of distal radius fractures in adults, although hematoma blocks appear to provide poorer analgesia and can compromise reduction.

A randomized trial identified 304 adults 60 and older with isolated, unstable distal radial fracture. The 187 preferring surgery were randomized to internal fixation, external fixation, or percutaneous pinning. Those preferring conservative therapy received casting. Internal fixation led to the fastest recovery, but at 12 months there were no differences in Michigan Hand Outcomes scores at 12 months between any of the 4 groups. While malunion was common with casting (48%) this seemed to have little impact on patient oriented outcomes.

An RCT of 461 patients with dorsally displaced fracture of the distal radius found no difference in functional outcomes between patients treated with Kirschner wires or volar locking plates. Kirschner wires, however, are less expensive and the procedure is faster. See .
For distal radius buckle fracture, a randomized trial concluded that home removal of a splint with physician follow-up as needed was non-inferior to physician follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks.

listitem.strong: Diaphyseal fracture of radius or ulna

list.listitem: Surgical indications and preferred techniques for diaphyseal fractures in the radius or ulna of children are not well supported by trial evidence.

A Cochrane review concluded that for patients undergoing surgery of the distal upper limb, multiple injection techniques for the brachial plexus were more effective than single or double injection techniques, although improvements in safety and clinical outcomes are not established.

In patients with unstable distal radial fracture, an RCT with 81 patients found that an accelerated rehab protocol focused on motion immediately post-op and early strengthening improved functional outcomes.

An RCT in 52 older patients with distal radial fracture randomized them to home hand strength exercises from 2 to 6 weeks or sham exercises. The hand strengthening group improved grip strength at 6 and 12 weeks.
See .
Randomized controlled trials have failed to establish the relative effectiveness of the various interventions used in the rehabilitation of adults with fractures of the distal radius. B

There is some evidence supporting the use of external fixation and pinning for distal radius fractures in adults, but their precise roles and methods have not been established, and it is unclear whether long-term outcomes will be consistently better. B
There is a high rate of removal or revision following radial head replacement in patients with unstable complex radius fractures. In one series, of 105 patients, 3 required revision and 26 removal.

A prospective cohort study of 81 children with Gartland type I to III supracondylar humeral fracture (mean 12 year follow-up) found generally good outcomes, although some patients had persistent pain, ulnar nerve sensitivity, and reduced grip strength and range of movement.
A randomized trial in 88 patients 60 years and older with a displaced 2 part humeral fracture found similar outcomes between surgical and conservative (sling or collar cuff for 3 weeks) management.

A randomized trial identified 304 adults 60 and older with isolated, unstable distal radial fracture. The 187 preferring surgery were randomized to internal fixation, external fixation, or percutaneous pinning. Those preferring conservative therapy received casting. Internal fixation led to the fastest recovery, but at 12 months there were no differences in Michigan Hand Outcomes scores at 12 months between any of the 4 groups. While malunion was common with casting (48%) this seemed to have little impact on patient oriented outcomes.
Casts extending above the elbow or below the elbow have comparable outcomes in children with uncomplicated forearm fractures. A Cochrane review confirms use of below the elbow casting.
A splint provides better functioning and similar pain relief compared with a plaster cast in children with distal radioulnar fractures, and refracture did not occur with either treatment.
Torus fractures of the radius in children may be treated with splints or casts, both with good clinical outcomes.
Salter-Harris (SH) fractures are fractures through the growth plates of children and adolescents. They are categorized depending on the involvement of the physis, metaphysis, and epiphysis. See .

cell.label: Immobilize arm with a standard sling or collar and cuff sling to prevent or limit sharp bone fragments from causing neurovascular injury. Provide effective analgesia (avoid opioids if patient has potential for hemodynamic or respiratory instability); tetanus toxoid, antibiotics as needed. Neurovascular compromise or fracture separation of the distal humeral epiphysis [1]?

Consider emergent reduction with effective analgesia: axillary block (risk of arterial or nerve injury), hematoma block (risk of osteomyelitis), intravenous regional anesthesia/Bier block (risk of lidocaine toxicity), inhaled nitrous oxide sedation (has variable efficacy), or conscious sedation (risk of respiratory depression, requires increased nursing time). Refer to orthopedic surgeon after emergent reduction [2].
Site of fracture?
Fracture of the anatomic neck, 2-part fracture, 3-part fracture, 4-part fracture, displaced fracture, fracture-dislocations, unstable joints, and/or neurovascular injury?
Refer immediately to orthopedic surgery [1-2].
1-Part Fractures Continue to immobilize arm in standard sling or collar and cuff sling; ice, NSAIDs; repeat evaluation and x-rays in 1 week [1-3]. Healing well clinically and on x-rays?
May start rehabilitation, as tolerated [4-5].

Reevaluate at 4 weeks, 6 weeks, 8 weeks, 12 weeks, and 16 weeks postinjury, instituting rehabilitation as tolerated, or referring to physical therapy if requiring assistance with exercises. Consider referral to orthopedic surgery if noted to have worsening pain or delayed healing at these follow-up visits [4-5].

More than 20 of anterior and posterior angulation, more than 30 varus, more than 1 inch or 2.5 cm of shortening, open fracture, presence of neurovascular injury, articular injury, ipsilateral forearm fracture, pathologic fracture, concomitant traumatic fracture, distal spiral shaft fracture [6-7]?
Refer immediately to orthopedic surgery [6-7].
Type of fracture?
Use coaptation or sugar-tong splint with a collar and cuff sling or a hanging cast [7].
Initiate weekly or biweekly follow-up visits until clinical and radiological union is evident, which may take from 8 to 14 weeks [6-8].
Consider referral to orthopedic surgery if with signs and symptoms of radial nerve injury, nonunion (clinical and radiological) [1-2, 7].
Apply coaptation or sugar tong splint and standard sling, allowing for shoulder motion [7].

- Initiate weekly or biweekly follow-up visits until clinical and radiological union is evident, which may take from 8 to 14 weeks [7-8] - On follow-up at 1-2 weeks postsplint application, apply a functional brace, as tolerated [7-8].
Child with displaced or extension-type fracture, unstable fractures, displaced fractures, or lateral condylar fractures, medial epicondylar fractures with more than 3-mm displacement [9]?
Refer immediately to orthopedic surgery [9].
Site of fracture?
Immobilize for 7 days, with elbow flexed at 90, forearm pronated, wrist flexed at 30 [10].
Immobilize with elbow in 90 of flexion, forearm in supination, wrist extended slightly to relax extensor muscles [10].
Splinting or casting in long arm cast for approximately 2 weeks, then hinged functional brace; early elbow motion [11-12].

Posterior splint, change to long arm cast with elbow in extension, when soft-tissue swelling has diminished. For extension-type fractures, place elbow 90 of flexion, with forearm in neutral rotation [12-13].

feature.caption: Forearm Fractures.
feature.feature_body:
Fracture Characteristics and Imaging
Nightstick fracture Isolated ulnar midshaft fracture.
Monteggia fracture Ulnar proximal one third fracture with radial head dislocation. Because isolated ulnar fractures are rare, always check for a Monteggia fracture. A line drawn through the radial shaft and head must always align with capitellum to rule out a dislocation.
Galeazzi fracture Fracture of the distal one third of radius with dislocation of distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ; "reverse Monteggia" fracture). Comparison views of uninjured forearm may be helpful. DRUJ injury is suggested by shortening of the radius by 5 mm, fracture of the ulnar styloid, widening of the DRUJ space by 2 mm, or subluxation of the DRUJ. False negative or false positive readings for DRUJ dislocation may result from a 10-20° rotation from normal radiographic position.
Concomitant radio-ulnar fracture Usually due to significant force or trauma. Swelling, deformity, straightforward radiographic diagnosis.
Essex-Lopresti fracture Fracture of the radial head and dislocation of DRUJ, with partial or complete disruption of radio-ulnar interosseous membrane.
Torus or greenstick fracture In children, from moderate degree of trauma. Incomplete fractures with cortical breaking on one side and/or bulging, or buckling of cortex.

feature.caption: Arm Fractures.
feature.feature_body:
Location of Fracture Characteristics/Considerations
Proximal humerus fractures - Shoulder trauma series useful: true anteroposterior (AP) view, axillary view or Velpeau view (arm in internal rotation, film taken superior to inferior as patient leans backward), and scapular Y view [1-2].
- CT scan useful if trauma series nondiagnostic [3].
Humeral midshaft fractures - Include shoulder and elbow x-rays if physical exam cannot exclude injury to those joints [2-3].
Distal humerus fractures - Characterize fracture fully in terms of bone quality, fracture pattern, level of comminution, articular involvement, displacement, and associated injuries before attempting treatment [4].
- Obtain AP radiographs with elbow flexed around 40°, with radiographic beam directed perpendicular to the distal humeral surface, allowing disengagement of olecranon from its fossa, giving better view of the distal humerus [2].
- In children, measure Baumann angle (angle between the lateral condylar physeal line and the axis of the humerus) with AP radiographs, and compare to contralateral side [2, 4-6].
- Displacement of the anterior, posterior, or supinator fat pad can suggest fracture, especially the posterior fat pad (up to 76% incidence of occult elbow fracture with a positive posterior fat pad sign) [6]. Suspect medial epicondylar fracture if fragment is visible within the joint and epicondyle is not visible [7]. CT scan can be obtained to further analyze fracture pattern [3].
- To check vascular status, order duplex Doppler ultrasonography or angiography [4]. Ultrasonography can differentiate stable from unstable pediatric lateral condylar fracture, and which nonossified fractures involve the joint surface and require operative intervention [6].
